name: Leadership in the Age of Agentic AI 3: Agentic AI, Automation and Leading Transformation
objectives: Given five processes in your area, map a process and score it as a first candidate for an AI agent, using the five factors: volume, clear steps, digital inputs, pain and low harm
For your pilot process, choose the agent's starting autonomy level, list every human approval point and name the agent owner, with approval before the agent spends money or speaks to customers

Given the people your pilot affects, plan how you will communicate with, involve and train them, saying honestly what will and will not change and how to raise concerns
For your team or organization, set up light AI governance with an inventory, an owner per agent and a review group, with at least three inventory rows and someone who can pause each agent

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Finding a process worth automating
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Map a process and score whether it is a good first candidate for an agent.
This lesson builds toward: Given five processes in your area, you will map a process and score it as a first candidate for an AI agent, using the five factors: volume, clear steps, digital inputs, pain and low harm.
Do not start with the technology; start with the work. A good first process is frequent, follows clear steps, uses information that is already digital, is annoying or slow for people, and has mistakes you can catch before they cause harm. Examples: sorting incoming requests, preparing weekly reports, scheduling, first drafts of routine replies.
Map it before you automate it. Write each step, who does it, the tool used and the time it takes. Mapping often shows waste you can remove with no AI at all. Automating a broken process just makes it break faster.
Score each candidate from 1 to 5 on: volume, clear steps, digital inputs, pain for staff, and low harm if wrong. Pick the highest total for your first pilot, not the most exciting idea. Avoid first pilots that make decisions about people, money or safety.
Step by step:
- List five candidate processes.
- Map the best two: steps, who, tool, time.
- Remove obvious waste first.
- Score each 1 to 5 on volume, clear steps, digital inputs, pain, low harm.
- Pick the highest score that avoids decisions about people, money or safety.
Words to know:
- Process map: a step-by-step picture of how a piece of work gets done today.
- Pilot: a small, time-limited trial before a wider rollout.
Try it now: List five processes in your area. Map the top two, score them on the five factors, and choose your pilot process.
You can now map a process and pick a sensible first candidate for an AI agent.

check.q: What does a process map show?
options: Each step, who does it, the tool used and the time it takes
check.why: A map shows how the work really happens, which reveals where an agent could help.

check.q: A process is rare, unclear and harmful if wrong. How would you score it as a first pilot?
options: A strong first pilot, because it is hard
A poor first candidate; pick a frequent, clear, low-harm process
Score it later, after the agent is built
check.why: First pilots should be frequent, clear and low harm if wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: How much may the agent do? Autonomy and approvals
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set an agent's level of autonomy and name the human approvals.
This lesson builds toward: For your pilot process, you will choose the agent's starting autonomy level, list every human approval point and name the agent owner, with approval before the agent spends money or speaks to customers.
Think of autonomy in levels. Level 1, suggest: the agent drafts, a person does everything. Level 2, prepare: the agent prepares the action (a filled-in form, a ready email) and a person approves each one. Level 3, act with checks: the agent acts on routine cases and sends exceptions to a person, who also reviews a sample. Level 4, act alone: rare, only for low-harm, reversible tasks.
Start pilots at level 1 or 2. Move up only when your measures show the agent is reliable, and only for the cases where it proved so. Keep approval before anything that spends money, speaks to customers or the public, changes records, or affects a person's rights.
Name an accountable person for the agent: someone who owns its results, reviews its log, and can switch it off. An agent with no owner is the most common way automation goes wrong.
Words to know:
- Autonomy level: how much an AI agent may do without a person approving.
- Exception: a case that does not fit the normal pattern and needs a person.
- Agent owner: the accountable person who owns an agent's results and can switch it off.
Try it now: For your pilot process, choose the starting autonomy level, list each step where a person must approve, and name the agent owner.
You can now set an agent's autonomy level, approval points and owner.

check.q: What does an agent owner do?
options: Owns the agent's results, reviews its logs and can switch it off
check.why: Every agent needs a named person who is accountable for it.

check.q: Your pilot agent will draft customer replies. What autonomy level would you start at?
options: Full autonomy, to save the most time
Act with checks, sending only exceptions
Level 1 or 2, so a person approves before anything reaches a customer
check.why: Pilots usually start low, and approval comes before an agent speaks to customers.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Measuring value and risk honestly
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set a baseline, success measures and a risk register for a pilot.
This lesson builds toward: Before the pilot starts, you will set a baseline, three to five success measures and a risk register, with quality measures and at least five risks, each with a guard and owner.
You cannot show improvement without a baseline: how the process performs today. Measure time per task, volume, error rate, waiting time and staff or customer satisfaction for a few weeks before the pilot.
Choose three to five success measures, and include quality, not just speed: "time per request down 30 percent with no rise in errors". Count the hidden costs: review time, tool costs, training and the time to fix agent mistakes.
Keep a risk register: a simple table of each risk, how likely it is, how bad it would be, the guard, and the owner. Typical agent risks: wrong outputs, privacy leaks, prompt injection, too much access, unfair outcomes, staff over-trusting the agent, and vendor lock-in. NIST's free AI Risk Management Framework, organized as Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, is a good guide.
Step by step:
- Measure the baseline for a few weeks.
- Pick three to five measures, including quality.
- Count hidden costs: review, tools, training, fixes.
- List at least five risks in a register.
- Give each risk a guard and an owner.
Words to know:
- Baseline: how a process performs before you change it.
- Risk register: a table of risks with how likely, how bad, the guard and the owner.
- Vendor lock-in: being stuck with one supplier because switching is hard.
Official sources:
- NIST AI Risk Management Framework
Try it now: Write the baseline measures for your pilot process, three to five success measures, and a risk register with at least five risks, each with a guard and owner.
You can now set a baseline, honest success measures and a risk register for an AI pilot.

options: A list of risks, each with likelihood, impact, guard and owner
A list of staff who use AI
check.why: A risk register makes each risk visible and gives it a guard and an owner.

check.q: Your only success measure is "faster". What would you add?
options: A quality measure, such as no rise in errors
A measure of how much staff like the vendor
The agent's own rating of itself
check.why: Speed without quality can hide errors and rework.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Leading the people and the plan

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Leading people through change
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan how you will communicate, involve and train the people affected.
This lesson builds toward: Given the people your pilot affects, you will plan how you will communicate with, involve and train them, saying honestly what will and will not change and how to raise concerns.
Automation changes jobs, and people feel it before you announce anything. Involve the people who do the work today from the start: they know the exceptions, the workarounds and the real risks. They should help map the process and test the agent.
Communicate early and honestly: why you are piloting, what will and will not change, what happens to the time saved, and how people can raise concerns. If you do not know yet, say so and say when you will know. Silence fills with rumors.
Plan the new skills: reviewing agent work, handling exceptions, spotting AI errors and writing good instructions. Budget time for training, and recognize people who find problems; catching an agent's mistake is a contribution, not disloyalty.
Step by step:
- List who is affected and how.
- Invite the people who do the work to help map and test.
- Tell them why, what changes, what does not, and how to raise concerns.
- Plan the new skills and the training time.
- Recognize people who find problems.
Words to know:
- Change management: planning how people move from the old way of working to the new one.
- Stakeholder: anyone affected by or able to affect a change.
Try it now: List the people your pilot affects. Write a short first message to them that explains why, what will and will not change, and how to raise concerns. Plan one training session.
You can now plan the people side of an AI change: involvement, honest communication and training.

options: Moving people from the old way of working to the new one
check.why: Change management is about people, not just tools.

check.q: Staff ask whether the pilot will affect their jobs and you do not know yet. What do you say?
options: Say you do not know yet and when you will know
check.why: Honest answers, even "not yet", build trust during change.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Simple AI governance that works
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up light governance: an inventory, an owner per agent and a review rhythm.
This lesson builds toward: For your team or organization, you will set up light AI governance with an inventory, an owner per agent and a review group, with at least three inventory rows and someone who can pause each agent.
Governance means deciding who may do what with AI, and checking it is working. It does not have to be heavy. Start with three things.
An inventory: a list of every AI tool and agent in use, what it does, what data it touches, its autonomy level and its owner. You cannot govern what you do not know exists, and staff often start using tools on their own.
A small review group (for a small organization, two or three people) that approves new agents, reviews the risk register and incident reports monthly, and can pause any agent. Write down how someone reports an AI problem and how fast you respond. Check any laws or rules that apply to your sector and location with a qualified advisor.
Step by step:
- Build an inventory of AI tools and agents.
- Record purpose, data, autonomy level and owner for each.
- Form a small review group.
- Review risks and incidents monthly; allow any agent to be paused.
- Publish how to report an AI problem.
Words to know:
- Governance: the rules and roles for deciding and checking how something is used.
- Inventory: a complete list of the AI tools and agents in use.
- Incident: an event where something went wrong or nearly did.
Official sources:
- NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern function)
Try it now: Start an AI inventory for your team with at least three rows (tool, purpose, data, autonomy level, owner). Name who would be in your review group.
You can now set up light AI governance with an inventory, owners and a review rhythm.

options: A list of every AI tool and agent in use, with owners
A list of staff trained in AI
check.why: You cannot govern what you have not listed.

check.q: You are unsure which laws apply to your agent in your sector. What would you do?
options: Ask the AI assistant and follow it
Assume no laws apply to pilots
check.why: Laws differ by sector and location, so a qualified advisor should confirm them.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing the 90-day pilot plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Assemble a 90-day pilot plan with a go or no-go rule.
This lesson builds toward: Using the parts above, you will write and present a two-page 90-day pilot plan with a go or no-go rule, with the rule written before the pilot starts and two hard questions recorded.
Pull your work together into a two-page plan. Days 1 to 30: baseline, set-up, training, agent at level 1 or 2 on a small share of the work. Days 31 to 60: run, review the log weekly, fix problems, track measures. Days 61 to 90: compare with the baseline, interview staff and decide.
Write the go or no-go rule before you start, so the result decides, not enthusiasm: "Scale to the whole team if time per request falls at least 25 percent, errors do not rise, and no serious incident occurs. Otherwise stop or redesign." Include a stop rule for serious incidents at any time.
Use an AI assistant to turn your notes into a clean draft, then edit it yourself. Present it in five minutes: the problem, the process, the agent and its limits, measures, risks, people plan, and the decision rule.
Step by step:
- Days 1-30: baseline, set-up, training, small start.
- Days 31-60: run, weekly log review, fixes, measures.
- Days 61-90: compare, interview staff, decide.
- Write the go or no-go rule and the stop rule first.
- Draft with AI, edit yourself, present in five minutes.
Words to know:
- Go or no-go rule: a decision rule, written in advance, for whether to continue.
- Stop rule: a condition that pauses the pilot at once, such as a serious incident.
Try it now: Final task: write your two-page 90-day pilot plan with process map, autonomy and approvals, owner, baseline and measures, risk register, people plan, and go or no-go rule. Present it to a colleague in five minutes and write down their two hardest questions.
You can now lead an AI agent pilot from idea to a plan with clear measures, guardrails and a decision rule.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Process map The current steps or times are missing. Shows the current steps, who does them and the time. Notes waste found while mapping and why this process scored well. Autonomy and approvals No autonomy level, approval points or accountable person. States the agent's job, its autonomy level, every human approval point and the accountable person. Explains why that level fits a first pilot. Measures and risks No baseline, or fewer than five risks. Baseline and success measures, and a risk register with at least five risks. Every risk has a guard and an owner, and measures include quality. People plan Does not say who is affected or how they will be told and trained. Names who is affected and how you will communicate and train. Involves staff in mapping and testing and says how to raise concerns. Go or no-go rule No rule, or one that cannot be measured. A clear go or no-go rule for day 90, written before the start. Includes a stop rule for serious incidents during the pilot. Presented and tested Not presented, or questions not recorded. Presented in five minutes with the colleague's two hardest questions written down. The plan was updated to answer those questions. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a go or no-go rule?
options: A rule for when staff may use AI
A rule written in advance that decides whether to scale up, change or stop at day 90
check.why: Writing the rule first keeps the day-90 decision honest.

check.q: A colleague asks a hard question about your plan that you cannot answer. What do you do?
options: Write it down and add the answer or a next step to the plan
Remove that part of the plan
check.why: Hard questions show where the plan needs work before the pilot starts.
